title: ¡Qué Sorpresa!

jokes.text: I said everyone, Sketch-Tron 6000.
jokes.setup: Jack is calling the entire staff to attention for an important announcement.
jokes.punchline: He has to specifically call out 'Sketch-Tron 6000' by name, implying a robot is part of the writing staff and is ignoring him.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical cold-open joke. The absurdity of a robot named 'Sketch-Tron 6000' being a normal member of the writing staff, delivered with zero acknowledgment by Jack, is classic 30 Rock world-building. High originality for casual delivery of insane premise.

jokes.text: Tracy, do not mention where you think dinosaurs come from. Do not mention the underwater city of Sauronicon.
jokes.setup: Jack is instructing staff to behave normally for the Kabletown owner's visit.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has such specific and insane beliefs (dinosaur origins theory, underwater city of Sauronicon) that Jack has to pre-emptively list them as forbidden topics.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific comedy. The joke works on two levels: first, we laugh at the absurdity of the content (Sauronicon); second, we laugh that Jack knows Tracy well enough to have a prepared list. 'Sauronicon' is a great invented word. High character integration — this could only be Tracy.

jokes.text: Jenna, get all of your crazy yelling out of your system. 'If you don't volumize my hair, I will choke you to death with your boyfriend's wig!'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Jenna to get her 'crazy yelling' out before the visit.
jokes.punchline: Jenna obliges with an unhinged, hyper-specific threat involving her hairdresser's boyfriend's wig — a threat so specific it implies this situation has happened before.
jokes.explanation: The hyper-specificity is what elevates this — 'your boyfriend's wig' adds a layer of detail that makes it feel like a real threat from Jenna's real life. Jack's breezy 'Very good' reaction sells it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Frank, how is your armpit thing? Not great. It's almost touching my thigh thing.
jokes.setup: Jack is doing a quick check-in on everyone's normalcy before the visit.
jokes.punchline: Frank has an 'armpit thing' — some kind of grotesque bodily growth — and it's progressing toward his thigh.
jokes.explanation: Rapid-fire gross-out delivered with total normalcy. The vagueness of 'armpit thing' and 'thigh thing' is funnier than specificity would be here. Economy is the main virtue — it's two lines.

jokes.text: Remember, everyone, just don't be yourselves.
jokes.setup: Jack has been giving everyone specific instructions to suppress their personalities.
jokes.punchline: He summarizes with the devastatingly blunt 'just don't be yourselves' — the inverse of motivational-speaker wisdom, said with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the opening scene. Works as an ironic inversion of a common platitude, and the economy is near-perfect — five words that summarize the entire preceding sequence. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, do you need sex advice? Here's a tip. Sometimes a lady likes to leave her blazer on.
jokes.setup: Jack says he needs to ask Liz something in private, setting up an expectation of a serious conversation.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately assumes it's a sex question and offers the deeply unglamorous tip that 'sometimes a lady likes to leave her blazer on' — simultaneously revealing her own frumpy self-image.
jokes.explanation: A gem. The misdirection is excellent — we expect something serious, and Liz's eagerness to give sex advice is already funny. But 'sometimes a lady likes to leave her blazer on' is the perfect punchline: unglamorous, defensive, deeply Liz Lemon, and delivered with total confidence. This joke could only come from this character.

jokes.text: Without us, who would present awards to actors?
jokes.setup: Tracy/Jenna receives a gift bag and says 'actors deserve gifts.'
jokes.punchline: The follow-up question — 'Without us, who would present awards to actors?' — is a perfectly circular piece of actor logic that reveals complete self-absorption.
jokes.explanation: The circular logic ('who would present awards TO actors?') is an excellent piece of celebrity self-absorption comedy. The argument is tautological in a way that sounds almost reasonable for half a second before collapsing.

jokes.text: So... which one of us is going to get this computer? Just kidding. We both are!
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna open a gift bag that apparently contains computers.
jokes.punchline: The pause implying fierce competition is instantly deflated — 'Just kidding. We both are!' — but the setup reveals how naturally competitive they are.
jokes.explanation: Functional comic beat that sets up the sweatshirt running gag. The subversion is mild — the self-aware 'Just kidding' is a bit too on-the-nose. Serviceable.

jokes.text: The box would make a perfect coffin for my Teddy Bear.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna are marveling at their gift computers.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's first thought about the computer box is that it would be a perfect coffin for his teddy bear — implying the teddy bear has died or will die.
jokes.explanation: Quick dark absurdist beat. Tracy's childlike ownership of a teddy bear combined with the grim pragmatism of already planning its coffin is a neat character joke. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: When we met four years ago, we were fighting about the silliest things... Dressing rooms, air time, you coming in and ruining my show... You taking my nephew's virginity.
jokes.setup: Tracy/Jenna are having a touching reflective moment about their relationship growth.
jokes.punchline: The list of 'silly things' escalates from petty TV disputes to 'you taking my nephew's virginity' — which is then categorized as equally silly.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed list escalation. The structure is classic — establish a pattern of small petty complaints, then detonate with an enormous one delivered at the same level of gravity. 'You taking my nephew's virginity' being lumped in as 'silly' is the key subversion.

jokes.text: There's only one. You take it. I don't care. I want you to selfishly take the best sweatshirt in the world.
jokes.setup: After the touching moment of apparent harmony, they discover there is only one sweatshirt in the gift bag.
jokes.punchline: One of them says 'I don't care' and then immediately reveals the opposite with 'I want you to selfishly take the best sweatshirt in the world' — dripping with barely-contained resentment.
jokes.explanation: The setup of their newly achieved 'harmony' being immediately shattered by a single sweatshirt is a great structural joke. The passive-aggressive phrasing is very well-written — 'selfishly take' is a great word choice.

jokes.text: ...a tiny desk with a miniature pen set on it.
jokes.setup: Jack is listing normal baby items Liz should help Avery shop for: a crib, small clothes...
jokes.punchline: He includes 'a tiny desk with a miniature pen set on it' — an absurdly adult corporate accessory for a newborn, revealing Jack's mindset that babies are simply small executives.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Jack Donaghy joke. The escalation from normal baby items to 'a tiny desk with a miniature pen set on it' is brilliantly character-specific — Jack conceives of babies as small future executives. The specificity of the pen set makes it far funnier than just 'a tiny desk.' This joke could not be told by any other character on any other show.

jokes.text: I assumed Avery would have a terrifying best friend she'd do stuff like that with.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz to take Avery shopping for baby things because she doesn't have a close friend to do it with.
jokes.punchline: Liz assumed someone like Avery would have a 'terrifying best friend' — implying that powerful, beautiful women travel in packs of equally intimidating women.
jokes.explanation: A solid observational joke about social dynamics. 'Terrifying best friend' is a good phrase. Liz's outsider perspective on how glamorous people operate is a recurring theme that lands here.

jokes.text: Avery does have a sister, but Eugenia is currently institutionalized for nerves... Lesbian...
jokes.setup: Jack explains why Avery can't ask family members to help.
jokes.punchline: He mentions Eugenia is institutionalized 'for nerves' then pauses and quietly adds '...Lesbian' — implying the sister's lesbianism is either the real reason, or an additional complication, delivered with Jack's patrician obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: The pause and the quiet, additional disclosure of 'Lesbian' as a separate, almost equal concern — delivered in Jack's clipped patrician manner — is a masterclass in character-specific comedy. It satirizes a certain class of old-money conservatism where both things are genuine problems. The structure (long reason, pause, single-word addition) is perfect.

jokes.text: Michael Kors is a friend. We own a gay racehorse together. And I convinced him to make wizard cloaks fashionable for ladies this winter.
jokes.setup: Jack explains how Avery has been hiding her pregnancy — through fashion.
jokes.punchline: The explanation involves co-owning a 'gay racehorse' with Michael Kors and convincing him to make 'wizard cloaks' fashionable — a cascade of absurd specifics delivered as mundane facts.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Gay racehorse' is a standalone absurdist gem — the adjective is doing enormous work. 'Wizard cloaks fashionable for ladies' is brilliantly specific and visual. The whole package is delivered as if it's completely normal networking. High originality, very Jack-specific, highly quotable. This is 30 Rock operating at peak form.

jokes.text: It's my fault for asking.
jokes.setup: Jack has just explained the gay racehorse and wizard cloaks.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defeated 'It's my fault for asking' is the perfect straight-man reaction — she accepts responsibility for having prompted the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the wizard cloaks absurdity. Liz's relationship to Jack's world — simultaneously exasperated and resigned — is perfectly captured in five words.

jokes.text: Ah, see, that would never happen if men could get pregnant. Which is the premise of my one-act play The Seahorses of Warwickshire Abbey.
jokes.setup: Jack explains that Avery could lose her job if her pregnancy is discovered by a rival.
jokes.punchline: Liz makes a feminist observation and then reveals she's already written a one-act play about it, titled 'The Seahorses of Warwickshire Abbey' — an absurdly literary, pseudo-Downton-Abbey title for what is presumably a very earnest feminist seahorse drama.
jokes.explanation: Excellent. The joke works on multiple levels: Liz's earnest feminism, her delusion that she's a playwright, and the specific title 'The Seahorses of Warwickshire Abbey' which is funny both for the highbrow pretension and the absurdity of seahorses in a period drama setting. Strong character integration — this is peak Liz Lemon intellectual vanity.

jokes.text: And that's not racist because I don't know what she is.
jokes.setup: Jack has said Carmen Chao is 'sneaky' — a racially loaded adjective.
jokes.punchline: Jack preemptively defends himself from racism accusations with the logic that it can't be racist if he doesn't know her ethnicity — which is itself a satirical skewering of a certain kind of bad-faith anti-racism defense.
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of satirical comedy about how people rationalize prejudice. Jack's confident, circular logic ('I can't be racist if I don't know what she is') is both funny and a genuine critique. Very Jack.

jokes.text: Man, we all lead such complicated lives. Hey, do you want to go to that new popcorn place for lunch?
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz have just discussed a complex situation involving pregnancy secrecy and career threats.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately follows 'we all lead such complicated lives' with an invitation to a popcorn restaurant — an immediate and total deflation of the philosophical weight she just assigned the situation.
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon structure — builds to mock-profundity, immediately undercuts it with food. The juxtaposition is clean and well-timed.

jokes.text: You can tell a lot about someone by their handshake. You are confident. And you ate dinner in front of a mirror last night.
jokes.setup: Jack claims you can tell a lot about a person from their handshake.
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates on Liz, correctly (probably) identifying her confidence level and then somehow knowing she ate dinner in front of a mirror — a deeply specific and sad detail that Liz doesn't deny.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The escalation from a reasonable observation ('you are confident') to the absurdly specific and melancholy 'you ate dinner in front of a mirror last night' is perfectly structured. The detail is both surprising and completely believable for Liz. It works as character comedy, absurdism, and a tiny gut-punch about Liz's loneliness. Liz's non-denial in the next beat makes it even better.

jokes.text: Carol's away a lot.
jokes.setup: Jack has just diagnosed that Liz eats dinner alone in front of a mirror. This is a brief talking-head/aside.
jokes.punchline: Liz's only response/explanation is the soft, sad 'Carol's away a lot' — confirming the mirror detail without addressing how Jack knew, and adding pathos.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in economy. Three words that confirm the joke, add character depth, and generate pathos. The loneliness of 'Carol's away a lot' delivered as a non-defensive explanation is deeply Liz Lemon. The talking-head format makes it funnier — she's confessing this to no one.

jokes.text: I'm no 'sir,' Jack. Call me Hank. Or 'hey, idiot,' like my wife does. I'm kidding. She's an angel.
jokes.setup: Jack formally addresses Hank as 'sir,' establishing a power dynamic.
jokes.punchline: Hank deflects with folksy charm and self-deprecating humor ('hey, idiot, like my wife does') before immediately undermining the joke with 'I'm kidding, she's an angel' — a man who can't even commit to a joke about his wife.
jokes.explanation: Efficient character establishment for Hank — folksy, anti-hierarchical, slightly awkward. The self-correction ('I'm kidding, she's an angel') is a good touch that makes him feel real and slightly bumbling. Contrasts well with Jack's formality.

jokes.text: No, it's fine, Jack. Kabletown's a family company, and where I come from, families eat together. This is no longer the executive dining room. It's the Everyone dining room.
jokes.setup: Jack is clearly irritated that the dining room has been opened to everyone. Hank reframes it positively.
jokes.punchline: The renaming from 'executive dining room' to 'the Everyone dining room' — delivered with genuine enthusiasm — is a joke about the gap between corporate egalitarianism as performance and corporate reality.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy that establishes Hank's corporate philosophy and Jack's discomfort. The joke is more setup for later conflict than a standalone punchline.

jokes.text: This is where we used to hold retirement parties. The balcony below is probably still littered with stripper bones.
jokes.setup: Jack is playing tour guide for Hank, describing the former executive dining room.
jokes.punchline: The casual mention that the balcony is 'probably still littered with stripper bones' — said as a normal historical footnote — implies decades of depraved executive parties with no apparent guilt.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. 'Stripper bones' as a casual, historical observation — 'probably still littered' implies Jack hasn't checked, nor does he feel he needs to — is perfectly Jack Donaghy. The dark implication is enormous but the delivery is breezy. High quotability.

jokes.text: And now there are people here wearing sandals. Yeah. Isn't that nice?
jokes.setup: Jack has just noted the stripper bones; Hank is cheerfully positive about the open dining room.
jokes.punchline: Jack's horror at 'people wearing sandals' in the executive space is the punchline — for Jack, this is a catastrophe equivalent to the stripper bones. Hank's oblivious 'Isn't that nice?' makes it better.
jokes.explanation: The comic contrast between Jack's world (stripper bones = acceptable; sandals = unacceptable) is the real joke. The parallel delivery makes both elements funnier.

jokes.text: The original name for the DVR was 'The Thing Carlos Thought Of.'
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining his company philosophy — that the best ideas come from regular employees, using his driver Carlos as an example.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the DVR was originally called 'The Thing Carlos Thought Of' — a non-name that became a proper name — is a great absurdist detail about how a genuine populist culture looks from the inside.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever piece of absurdist worldbuilding. The specificity of the placeholder name becoming a real working title is both believable and ridiculous. It establishes Hank's character while being funny on its own terms.

jokes.text: I'll be the guy wearing the Bugs Bunny tie.
jokes.setup: Hank wraps up his pitch about employee idea day and tells Jack he'll check in.
jokes.punchline: He identifies himself with 'the Bugs Bunny tie' — implying he wears a cartoon character tie as a matter of course, which is confirmed as a rewatch detail.
jokes.explanation: Quick character-building visual joke. The Bugs Bunny tie is the kind of detail that makes Hank a fully realized comedic foil to Jack — a powerful man with no pretension whatsoever.

jokes.text: What is this green stuff? Wipe it off. Wipe it off!
jokes.setup: Hank has been eating the food in the 'Everyone dining room.'
jokes.punchline: He has eaten something unidentifiable and reacts with physical disgust — a sudden break from his folksy pleasantness that suggests even he has limits.
jokes.explanation: Mild physical comedy beat. Functional but not particularly clever — the joke is essentially 'he ate something gross.' Gets a mild chuckle as a character beat.

jokes.text: These pregnancy photos are so tacky. They're like those knockoff bags you get in Chinatown. 'I like pradort bag.'
jokes.setup: Carmen and Avery are apparently at a store or event with pregnancy photos displayed.
jokes.punchline: Carmen's dismissal of pregnancy photos as knockoff Chinatown bags is catty and specific; the payoff 'I like pradort bag' is a mispronunciation joke implying Carmen does buy knockoff bags and knows it.
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining quality of the joke — Carmen compares something to knockoff bags and then reveals she buys knockoff bags — is a nice structural touch. 'Pradort' is a good invented mispronunciation.

jokes.text: I love their creepy little hands and the way they crawl fast, like a rat monster.
jokes.setup: Carmen claims to love babies.
jokes.punchline: Her description of what she loves about babies — 'creepy little hands' and 'the way they crawl fast, like a rat monster' — reveals she actually finds babies somewhat horrifying.
jokes.explanation: 'Like a rat monster' is an excellent phrase — unexpected, specific, and slightly horrifying. It characterizes Carmen as someone who performs warmth while being fundamentally unsettling.

jokes.text: Some dude jacked me, and now his sperm is growing in my stomach.
jokes.setup: Liz is improvising a cover story for Avery, claiming to be the pregnant one.
jokes.punchline: Her description of pregnancy — 'some dude jacked me, and now his sperm is growing in my stomach' — is hilariously clinical and crude simultaneously, completely wrong medically, and delivered with confidence.
jokes.explanation: A fantastic Liz Lemon improvisation. The language is simultaneously too crude and medically wrong ('his sperm is growing in my stomach'), delivered with complete confidence. Carmen's horrified 'That's not how babies are made' is the perfect reaction. Strong character integration — only Liz would phrase it this way.

jokes.text: That's not how babies are made.
jokes.setup: Liz has just described pregnancy in a completely wrong and crude way.
jokes.punchline: Carmen's flat, factual correction — delivered as pure deadpan — is funnier than any elaborate comeback.
jokes.explanation: A perfect reaction beat. The flatness of the correction — no disbelief, no outrage, just a factual statement — is the joke. Economy is maximal.

jokes.text: So by the law of verbal traps, you have to do it.
jokes.setup: Carmen has maneuvered Avery into agreeing with her story idea before revealing she's a subject.
jokes.punchline: Carmen invokes 'the law of verbal traps' — a completely made-up legal principle she states with full confidence — as if it's a recognized journalistic or legal doctrine.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. 'The law of verbal traps' is a made-up doctrine stated with total confidence that both characterizes Carmen as manipulative and is funny on its own as an absurdist legal concept. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Fine. I'll just go to the popcorn place alone, even though all their advertising suggests it is a place for groups of friends to have a good time.
jokes.setup: Carmen demands the interview happen at Liz's office rather than the popcorn restaurant Liz wanted to go to.
jokes.punchline: Liz's passive-aggressive complaint about going to the popcorn place alone, citing the restaurant's own advertising as evidence of her social failure, is a beautiful piece of Liz Lemon self-pity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Liz Lemon moments. The specificity of citing advertising copy as evidence of her own social isolation is brilliant. It captures Liz's self-awareness, self-pity, and food obsession simultaneously. The phrase 'all their advertising suggests' is the key — it's such a bizarre and precise way to articulate loneliness. Highly quotable, very rewatch-worthy.

jokes.text: Good sweatshirt to you. How are you sweatshirting this sweatshirt?
jokes.setup: Tracy encounters Jenna wearing the contested sweatshirt.
jokes.punchline: Tracy greets Jenna using 'sweatshirt' as a noun, verb, and adjective in rapid succession — turning the object of obsession into an entire language system.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's linguistic creativity in using 'sweatshirt' as every part of speech is a great absurdist character moment. It shows both his obsession and his odd intelligence. Part of the episode's running gag about the sweatshirt.

jokes.text: I want that sweatshirt! No. You can't take this away from me, like you took away my show. And my grandmother's jewelry chest.
jokes.setup: Tracy is confronting Jenna over the sweatshirt.
jokes.punchline: Tracy escalates from the sweatshirt to 'my show' to 'my grandmother's jewelry chest' — a cascade of grievances where the level of injury seems to keep escalating past and below the sweatshirt.
jokes.explanation: Standard Tracy escalation joke. The grandmother's jewelry chest is the best detail — it implies Jenna also stole from Tracy's grandmother, which is a wild implication treated as normal. Functional.

jokes.text: Was I supposed to throw up in something of mine?
jokes.setup: Tracy has accused Jenna of taking his grandmother's jewelry chest.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's response — 'Was I supposed to throw up in something of mine?' — is an incomprehensible non-sequitur that simultaneously defends the jewelry chest theft (she used it as a vomit receptacle) and makes everything worse.
jokes.explanation: A superb joke. The reveal that Jenna used a grandmother's jewelry chest as a vomit receptacle, delivered with defensive reasonableness, is gloriously absurd. 'Was I supposed to throw up in something of mine?' implies she has a surplus of vomit situations in her life. Very Jenna. High originality, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Stop! Sweatshirty is a boy!
jokes.setup: Tracy attempts to take the sweatshirt from Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Jenna screams 'Stop! Sweatshirty is a boy!' — having named and gendered the sweatshirt, escalating the absurdity of the running gag.
jokes.explanation: The humanization of the sweatshirt by naming it 'Sweatshirty' and assigning it a gender is a great absurdist escalation. Economy is near-perfect — four words that deliver maximum absurdity.

jokes.text: Is she doing an expose on how feminism has led to a happiness crisis among educated women?
jokes.setup: Kenneth informs Liz that Carmen Chao called about an interview.
jokes.punchline: Liz's first assumption about any possible story about her — that it's a feminist think-piece about unhappy educated women — reveals both her self-image and her media-literacy about what stories typically target women like her.
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of meta-commentary delivered as character comedy. The specificity of 'happiness crisis among educated women' both parodies a real media trend and illuminates Liz's self-image. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Lemon told me this morning she got jacked big time.
jokes.setup: Tracy is sharing gossip that Liz is pregnant.
jokes.punchline: Tracy uses his own crude phrasing 'got jacked big time' — a callback to Liz's own earlier crude description — to spread the pregnancy rumor with unintentional vulgarity.
jokes.explanation: An effective callback that shows how Liz's crude improvised description has filtered through Tracy and been made even more inappropriate. Good running gag payoff.

jokes.text: I will make a good first impression, so I need all of you to be your most normal... Well, it is called. I am telling everyone here that there's no way I could be pregnant because I have had my period for the last 61 days.
jokes.setup: Jack is pleading with Liz to keep the pregnancy story going; Liz is threatening to blow it by oversharing.
jokes.punchline: Liz's proposed solution to ending the rumor — announcing to everyone that she's been having her period for 61 days — is both medically alarming and deeply inappropriate as office communication.
jokes.explanation: Liz's complete lack of filter around bodily information is a classic character trait, and '61 days' is a hilariously specific detail (also medically alarming). The oversharing as workplace communication is the perfect Liz Lemon move.

jokes.text: Don Geiss gave me this watch for firing a man on his deathbed!
jokes.setup: Jack is spiraling about whether he has a future at Kabletown under Hank Hooper's folksy management style.
jokes.punchline: Jack holds up his watch as a credential — but the achievement it commemorates (firing a dying man) is horrifying, delivered with complete pride.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Jack Donaghy joke. The watch-as-credential is a standard executive flex, but the credential itself — firing a man on his deathbed — is darkly horrifying and delivered with pure pride. It's a perfect encapsulation of Jack's character and values. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: How come when I try to get you to go to a murder-mystery party with me, it's all, 'we're business colleagues, Lemon'? Ugh, I don't know why I ever chose you as a friend. Let's just be clear about this — I chose you.
jokes.setup: Jack has asked Liz, 'as a friend,' to continue faking a pregnancy to help Avery.
jokes.punchline: Liz calls out Jack's selective deployment of the word 'friend,' then Jack immediately reclaims the power dynamic: 'I chose you.'
jokes.explanation: A strong two-part joke about the Jack/Liz friendship dynamic. Liz's murder-mystery party grievance is funny as a specific detail, and Jack's instant power reclamation — 'I chose you' — is both funny and a perfect encapsulation of their relationship's asymmetry. Well-structured.

jokes.text: I heard the blessed news, Liz. May I kiss your stomach? Hello, beautiful. It's Uncle Wutzy.
jokes.setup: The pregnancy rumor has spread to Kenneth, who approaches Liz with reverence.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's request to kiss Liz's stomach, followed by introducing himself to the fetus as 'Uncle Wutzy,' is deeply uncomfortable and very Kenneth — fervent, inappropriately intimate, and sweet in the most unsettling way.
jokes.explanation: 'Uncle Wutzy' is the perfect detail — the baby talk name combined with Kenneth's total sincerity makes it cringe-funny. Very strong character integration for Kenneth's particular brand of overwhelming earnestness.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, Jack, you and I have a pitch meeting later. You're a baby. Yes, you are. Yes, you're a baby...
jokes.setup: Tracy approaches Jack and Liz and seamlessly pivots from business to addressing the fictional baby.
jokes.punchline: Tracy transitions in one breath from a professional scheduling reminder to baby-talking at Liz's stomach — without any apparent awareness of the cognitive dissonance.
jokes.explanation: The pivot structure (professional → baby talk) in a single breath, with no transition or acknowledgment, is excellent. Tracy's seamlessness across radically different conversational registers is great character comedy.

jokes.text: So that's basically the show. And my sidekick is a hot black chick who can read minds.
jokes.setup: Employee pitch day is underway. An employee pitches a TV show concept.
jokes.punchline: The show pitch is indescribably vague 'so that's basically the show' followed by 'and my sidekick is a hot black chick who can read minds' — a throwaway detail of a generic TV character type.
jokes.explanation: The pitch montage is a meta-commentary on terrible TV concepts. 'Hot black chick who can read minds' is a succinct parody of network TV diversity box-checking. Functional satire.

jokes.text: We need a button that switches from pornography to basketball immediately. What you have isn't fast enough. My kids are starting to ask questions that I can't answer.
jokes.setup: Another employee pitches an idea to the executive team.
jokes.punchline: The pitch is for a faster porn-to-basketball switch, with the added reveal that his children are already asking questions — meaning they've caught him, repeatedly, and the current solution is too slow.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured and very funny pitch joke. The escalation — from the need for the button, to the reason ('not fast enough'), to the consequence ('kids asking questions') — builds perfectly. The implication that the current solution exists but is insufficient is the dark cherry on top.

jokes.text: So much of television is really not fit for children or Christians or the elderly. So what if there was a black bar on the lower half of your TV screen that kept you from seeing bad things? Like nudity, or soccer.
jokes.setup: An employee pitches a family-friendly content filter.
jokes.punchline: After listing legitimate objectionable content (nudity), the employee equates soccer with nudity as equally 'bad' — a non-sequitur that will become the episode's major running gag.
jokes.explanation: The 'soccer' addition is a perfect absurdist non-sequitur and sets up the episode's running gag about soccer being considered inappropriate content. 'Christians or the elderly' is also a funny grouping.

jokes.text: Congratulations. Worst so far!
jokes.setup: Jack has been suffering through terrible employee pitches all day.
jokes.punchline: Rather than being diplomatic, Jack gives the frank assessment 'Worst so far!' — delivered as if it's an encouraging milestone.
jokes.explanation: 'Congratulations. Worst so far!' is a great economy-of-language joke. The 'Congratulations' setup implies praise before the devastating pivot. Very Jack Donaghy. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Liz, I never get anything. All I want is one sweatshirt.
jokes.setup: Tracy approaches Liz with vulnerability about the sweatshirt situation.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's plaintive 'I never get anything. All I want is one sweatshirt' — despite being a wealthy famous person — is funny in its total lack of self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Serviceable continuation of the sweatshirt running gag. The pathos is the joke — Tracy genuinely believes he 'never gets anything' despite obvious wealth and fame. Functional but not the gag's strongest beat.

jokes.text: The story begins when dolphins ruled the earth.
jokes.setup: Tracy is apparently trying to explain his grievances about the sweatshirt situation.
jokes.punchline: Tracy begins a story with 'The story begins when dolphins ruled the earth' — a premise so cosmic and irrelevant that it could have no possible connection to a sweatshirt dispute.
jokes.explanation: A delight. 'The story begins when dolphins ruled the earth' is a magnificent opening line — confident, absurd, and deeply specific. It's a perfect encapsulation of Tracy Jordan's worldview and could easily be a standalone classic line. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: It'll turn the child into a Dracula.
jokes.setup: Tracy apologizes to Liz for stressing her out, noting it's bad for the fictional baby.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's concern for the baby manifests as the belief that stress turns children into 'a Dracula' — both the article 'a' and the noun choice are perfect.
jokes.explanation: The article 'a' before 'Dracula' is crucial — 'a Dracula' rather than 'a vampire' or 'Dracula' implies it's a recognized clinical category. Tracy's medical knowledge being filtered through monster mythology is quintessential Tracy Jordan. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Now, I will need to eat your umbilical cord.
jokes.setup: Tracy says he's not interested in godfather duties, then immediately reverses.
jokes.punchline: 'I will need to eat your umbilical cord' — stated as a firm requirement, with no explanation — is a deeply unsettling but hilarious piece of Tracy Jordan logic.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'I will NEED to eat your umbilical cord' — the 'need' implying genuine requirement rather than desire — is wonderful. No explanation is offered or expected. Tracy's ritual beliefs delivered with complete seriousness are a rich comedy vein, and this is a strong example.

jokes.text: Problem solved. Now no one gets it. Aw, man...
jokes.setup: The sweatshirt conflict has been escalating between Tracy and Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Liz resolves the conflict by destroying the sweatshirt — a perfect Solomon's judgment — and the devastated 'Aw, man...' shows that neither Tracy nor Jenna truly wanted the other to have it over themselves.
jokes.explanation: A clean structural resolution to the sweatshirt bit. The 'no one gets it' solution is a satisfying comedic callback to Solomon, and 'Aw, man' from presumably both of them is the right button. Solid.

jokes.text: Oh, that is like magic. People are nice to pregnant ladies.
jokes.setup: Liz is now playing the pregnancy angle for real, discovering the social benefits.
jokes.punchline: Liz's wonder at basic human kindness — 'that is like magic' — implies she normally experiences so little of it that strangers being nice to her is genuinely miraculous.
jokes.explanation: A gentle Liz Lemon self-deprecation moment. The 'like magic' reaction to ordinary kindness is the joke. Works but is relatively mild.

jokes.text: Remember, you're eating for two. Well, I guess two egg sandwiches... Times two is four.
jokes.setup: Someone reminds Liz she's 'eating for two' as a pregnant person.
jokes.punchline: Liz does the math in real time: two sandwiches per person, times two people, equals four sandwiches — a beautifully logical justification for gluttony.
jokes.explanation: A very strong Liz Lemon food joke. The math is presented as completely sincere — she's genuinely working it out and arrives at 'four' with satisfaction. The internal logic is airtight within Liz's worldview. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I'm a six sigma black belt ultra, with the groin branding to prove it.
jokes.setup: Jack is pushing back on Hank's casual management style by citing his own credentials.
jokes.punchline: Jack escalates the standard 'six sigma black belt' credential to 'ultra' and then adds 'with the groin branding to prove it' — implying a literal brand on his groin as a certification mark.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. 'Groin branding' as a professional certification is darkly absurd and completely Jack — he has submitted to physical suffering to prove corporate competence. The 'ultra' modifier on 'six sigma black belt' is also great. This is one of the episode's most quotable lines and perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: What's six sigma? Rock band?
jokes.setup: Jack has just cited his six sigma ultra credentials as evidence of his management superiority.
jokes.punchline: Hank doesn't know what six sigma is and guesses 'Rock band?' — completely puncturing Jack's pretension.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deflation of Jack's pomposity. 'Rock band?' as the guess is a great specific detail — not just 'I don't know what that is' but an active wrong guess that makes Jack's credential sound absurd.

jokes.text: First I want to go home and delete everything that's on my DVR. [TV MUTES] Oh, come on!
jokes.setup: Jack is continuing to struggle with the malfunctioning voice activation.
jokes.punchline: The TV interprets Jack's personal aside ('delete') as a command and mutes itself — the final indignity. Jack's 'Oh, come on!' is the button.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the malfunction escalation. The DVR reference is also a callback to Hank's earlier DVR story. Works as the final beat of the sequence.

jokes.text: Jack, it doesn't seem to work. You got any other notions, or should we jump to employee ideas?
jokes.setup: Jack's voice activation demo has been a complete disaster.
jokes.punchline: Hank's mild, gentle 'it doesn't seem to work' — the understatement of the century — combined with 'other notions' (an antiquated word choice) is a perfectly folksy deflation.
jokes.explanation: Hank's folksy understatement ('notions') works as character comedy and as a deflation of Jack's pretension. 'It doesn't seem to work' delivered without malice is the funniest possible response to the chaos.

jokes.text: What if you had a black bar at the bottom of the screen that prevented you from seeing anything dirty? ...Like soccer, or a woman stuffing a turkey.
jokes.setup: Desperate after his voice activation failure, Jack steals Kenneth's idea from the pitch session.
jokes.punchline: Jack recycles the employee's black bar pitch, but adds his own spin — 'a woman stuffing a turkey' as objectionable content alongside nudity and soccer.
jokes.explanation: The 'woman stuffing a turkey' addition is a great Jack-specific absurdist detail — what is objectionable about this? Is it sexual? Subversive? Jack delivers it with total confidence, making it funnier. Good callback to the earlier pitch.

jokes.text: You could call it 'Blabar.' A-plus work, Jack!
jokes.setup: Hank loves the stolen black bar idea and names it.
jokes.punchline: 'Blabar' — a clunky portmanteau of 'black bar' — is enthusiastically named by Hank with no irony. 'A-plus work, Jack!' completes the irony that Jack is being praised for an idea he stole.
jokes.explanation: 'Blabar' is funny as a bad brand name. The irony that Jack is being rewarded for theft is the structural joke. Hank's enthusiasm ('A-plus work!') is a funny character beat.

jokes.text: However, I presented it as my own idea. Wonderful! Next topic.
jokes.setup: Jack confesses to Kenneth that he stole his idea and expects some kind of reaction.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's immediate 'Wonderful! Next topic.' — total acceptance with no grievance — completely deflates Jack's prepared guilt trip.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's 'Wonderful! Next topic.' is a brilliant character joke. Jack has prepared a whole speech about leverage and opportunity, and Kenneth's complete non-reaction — delivered with genuine cheerfulness — exposes Jack's worldview as alien. The economy is exceptional. Very Kenneth.

jokes.text: Not what my uncle does when he gets a hitchhiker over a barrel, I'll tell you that.
jokes.setup: Jack says 'you have me over a barrel' and asks what Kenneth plans to do about it.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response — referencing what his uncle does when he gets a hitchhiker 'over a barrel' — implies something deeply sinister about his uncle's relationship with hitchhikers, delivered with complete Southern innocence.
jokes.explanation: A great dark joke delivered through Kenneth's characteristic obliviousness. The implication about the uncle is maximally dark, but Kenneth's cheerful tone implies he sees nothing wrong with it. This is Kenneth's particular comedy sweet spot — innocent delivery of horrifying content.

jokes.text: Last time I checked, best friends can't steal from each other. Now stop being a silly Simon.
jokes.setup: Jack insists that stealing Kenneth's idea is a business transaction Kenneth should exploit.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth reframes the theft as something that simply cannot happen between friends — a childlike moral framework — then adds 'silly Simon' as a gentle rebuke.
jokes.explanation: 'Silly Simon' as a rebuke directed at Jack Donaghy is a wonderful tonal incongruity. Kenneth's childlike ethics against Jack's corporate realpolitik is the episode's thematic spine, executed well here.

jokes.text: This isn't how it works! You're the one being a silly Simon!
jokes.setup: Kenneth has called Jack a 'silly Simon' for insisting on corporate power dynamics.
jokes.punchline: Jack, a powerful executive, reduces himself to shouting 'You're the one being a silly Simon!' — adopting Kenneth's childish framework in a moment of exasperation.
jokes.explanation: The callback where Jack uses Kenneth's own childish insult back at him is perfect. The image of Jack Donaghy — gravely serious executive — shouting 'You're the one being a silly Simon!' is hilarious and the delivery must be excellent. Strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: When are you due? April 20th, Hitler's birthday.
jokes.setup: Carmen ambushes Liz with pregnancy interview questions she must answer convincingly.
jokes.punchline: Liz's improvised due date — 'April 20th, Hitler's birthday' — is the worst possible thing to say, delivered immediately and with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Liz's improvisation going immediately to the darkest possible fact about a date is both character-specific and absurdly dark. The 'Hitler's birthday' annotation delivered as a completely normal aside is perfect — she's not trying to be dark, she just knows this fact and includes it automatically.

jokes.text: What's your pediatrician's name? / Dr. Rufus T. Barleysheath.
jokes.setup: Carmen is interrogating Liz about her fake pregnancy details.
jokes.punchline: Liz produces 'Dr. Rufus T. Barleysheath' — an extremely specific, Dickensian-sounding name that feels simultaneously too elaborate and too specific to be invented on the spot.
jokes.explanation: 'Rufus T. Barleysheath' is a masterwork of comedy naming. The middle initial, the 'T,' elevates it from funny to absurd. 'Barleysheath' sounds like something out of a Dickens novel, which makes it both too fake and somehow too specific. The name will be recalled later, adding rewatch value.

jokes.text: What's your pediatrician's name? Dr. Rufus T. Barleysheath. / What names are you considering? Rufus T. Barleysheath.
jokes.setup: Carmen is asking rapid-fire pregnancy questions, and Liz is improvising answers.
jokes.punchline: Liz uses the same invented name — 'Rufus T. Barleysheath' — for both the pediatrician AND the potential baby name. The repetition reveals the limit of Liz's improvisation.
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke. The name 'Rufus T. Barleysheath' is funny on its own (the formality of the middle initial T.), and using it for two different answers makes both funnier. The callback structure within the same rapid-fire exchange is well-timed.

jokes.text: Where was the baby conceived? In my vagina.
jokes.setup: Carmen is asking progressively more personal pregnancy questions to catch Liz out.
jokes.punchline: Liz's answer to 'where was the baby conceived?' — 'In my vagina' — is technically accurate but anatomically wrong as an answer to the question (which presumably means what location/city/etc.) and is delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed three-word joke. The misinterpretation of the question (geographic vs. anatomic) delivered with complete confidence is both funny and very Liz — she's technically right while being completely wrong. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Are you pregnant? No... way that I'm not.
jokes.setup: Carmen, still suspicious, asks Liz directly if she's pregnant.
jokes.punchline: Liz's answer 'No... way that I'm not' is a fumbled double negative that accidentally affirms she IS pregnant — a perfect linguistic pratfall.
jokes.explanation: The pause-and-correction structure of 'No... way that I'm not' is brilliantly written. Liz starts to say 'No' (the truth) then scrambles to correct it and creates a double negative that means the opposite. It's both linguistically clever and completely in character for Liz panicking under pressure.

jokes.text: She's a blonde. Don't you know there's a war going on? Or are you doing it for her old man husband? He's your boss. First of all, Jack means nothing to me. Shoot him in the throat and let the dogs eat him. I don't care.
jokes.setup: Carmen is interrogating Liz about why she's covering for Avery.
jokes.punchline: Carmen's escalation from 'there's a war going on' (between blondes and everyone else) to 'shoot him in the throat and let the dogs eat him' — as a way of expressing she doesn't care about Jack — is an enormous jump in violence delivered casually.
jokes.explanation: 'Shoot him in the throat and let the dogs eat him' is a vivid and extremely specific violent image delivered as an expression of indifference. The specificity is the joke. Carmen's character as someone who says unhinged things professionally is well-established here.

jokes.text: What's wrong with you? / Almost everything.
jokes.setup: Carmen is baffled by Liz's violent outburst about Jack.
jokes.punchline: 'Almost everything' — Liz's answer is honest, resigned, and delivered without self-pity.
jokes.explanation: Two words that do everything. 'Almost everything' as an answer to 'What's wrong with you?' is both self-deprecating and oddly dignified — the 'almost' qualifier implies she's thought about this and identified the limits of her dysfunction. Maximum economy. One of the episode's most quotable lines and a perfect Liz Lemon self-summary.

jokes.text: I thought it would be a fun visual if we got some b-roll of you taking sexy pregnancy photos where you bare your stomach like the pregnant bitch that you are.
jokes.setup: Carmen is ending the interview segment.
jokes.punchline: Carmen frames a demand for humiliating pregnancy photos in TV production language ('fun visual,' 'b-roll') while ending with 'the pregnant bitch that you are' — professional packaging around genuine hostility.
jokes.explanation: The incongruity between TV production language and personal hostility is the core joke. Carmen using 'b-roll' and 'fun visual' to describe a degrading request is a good character joke.

jokes.text: Innovation that is both family and bottom line friendly. Gentlemen, I give you Blabar. / You're really sexing me right now. It's filthy.
jokes.setup: Jack presents the stolen Blabar idea formally to the board.
jokes.punchline: Hank's response — 'You're really sexing me right now. It's filthy.' — uses the word 'sexing' in a corporate enthusiasm context that is simultaneously inappropriate and somehow folksy. His follow-up 'It's filthy' (meaning great) adds another layer.
jokes.explanation: 'You're really sexing me right now' as corporate enthusiasm language is a great Hank Hooper character joke. The double-take of 'It's filthy' used as positive is another layer. Good character work.

jokes.text: Jack! Jack! Jack! Jack! Jack...
jokes.setup: Something has happened with the pregnancy photo shoot that requires urgent Jack intervention.
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'Jack! Jack! Jack!' — escalating in desperation across what appears to be a long corridor chase — is a visual comedy beat where the comedy is Liz frantically chasing Jack.
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy beat that's difficult to fully assess from transcript alone. Likely works as a visual gag with Liz running through the building. Functional but relatively weak as pure dialogue.

jokes.text: One time, I saw a turtle...
jokes.setup: Jack has found Kenneth and is resuming their argument about the stolen idea during an intense moment.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, apparently in the middle of telling someone a story, only gets out 'One time, I saw a turtle...' before being interrupted — the incompleteness of the turtle anecdote being funnier than any completion could be.
jokes.explanation: The interrupted story is a great Kenneth joke — his innocent, small-town storytelling being cut off mid-turtle is both funny and sad. The turtle story will never be told. Economy is excellent — five words that generate both character and comedy.

jokes.text: Who the hell do you think you are?
jokes.setup: Jack enters dramatically to confront Kenneth.
jokes.punchline: Jack's aggressive 'Who the hell do you think you are?' — directed at Kenneth, arguably the least threatening person in any room — is a power-dynamic joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional beat that establishes Jack's aggression toward Kenneth. The joke is in the power imbalance but it's not particularly novel. Serviceable.

jokes.text: I can get you into a restaurant where you watch a child play with a bunny, then you eat the bunny.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to figure out what bribe would motivate Kenneth to demand something.
jokes.punchline: Jack offers exclusive access to a restaurant where the gimmick is — children playing with bunnies you then eat. The specificity and darkness, delivered as a desirable perk, is pure Jack Donaghy.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. The concept is extraordinary — a restaurant where children are made emotionally attached to bunnies that are then served for dinner. Jack offers this as a treat. The structure (watch a child play with a bunny → THEN you eat the bunny) is perfectly paced. 'Isn't that just Easter?' as Kenneth's response is the ideal button. High originality, exceptional character integration, extremely dark, and masterfully economical. Among the best Jack Donaghy jokes in the series.

jokes.text: Isn't that just Easter?
jokes.setup: Jack has offered access to the bunny restaurant as an elite perk.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's gentle, sincere 'Isn't that just Easter?' — treating the darkly elaborate restaurant as equivalent to a normal holiday — is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the bunny restaurant joke. 'Isn't that just Easter?' reframes the elite dark restaurant as a normal holiday tradition — implying Kenneth's family Easter involves the same dynamic. The economy is flawless (four words), the character integration is perfect (only Kenneth would say this, and mean it), and it turns a great joke into an all-time moment. This is the episode's highest-scoring joke.

jokes.text: Blackmail me. Demand to sleep with Avery. Hit me. Hit me in the face!
jokes.setup: Jack cannot process that Kenneth won't leverage the situation for personal gain, and escalates his demands.
jokes.punchline: Jack's escalating demands — from blackmail to sexual demands on his wife to 'hit me in the face' — reveal that Jack needs to be exploited because it's the only dynamic he understands.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant character comedy escalation. The joke is that Jack's entire framework for relationships is transactional, and Kenneth's genuine friendship breaks his brain. The escalation to 'hit me in the face' as a final, desperate offer is perfect. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, damn my krav maga training and lightning reflexes!
jokes.setup: Jack has ordered Kenneth to hit him; Kenneth tries, but Jack's instincts kick in.
jokes.punchline: Jack automatically blocks/deflects the punch due to his krav maga training and then curses himself for it — he genuinely wanted to be hit.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the 'hit me' escalation is excellent. Jack's krav maga training being so ingrained he can't even be hit on purpose — then his genuine frustration at his own competence — is a perfect joke. 'Damn my krav maga training and lightning reflexes!' is extremely quotable and a great line reading opportunity.

jokes.text: Release me, you hillbilly Circe! I am life. Revel in the glory of motherhood! Gaia flows through me. Rufus T. Barleysheath is kicking.
jokes.setup: Liz has apparently been pulled into the pregnancy photo shoot and is now posing with oiled stomach.
jokes.punchline: Liz has fully committed to the pregnancy role, shouting mythological proclamations ('Gaia flows through me!') while Avery tries to escape. 'Rufus T. Barleysheath is kicking' as a callback to her invented name is perfect.
jokes.explanation: 'Hillbilly Circe' is a great insult — both classical and regional. 'Gaia flows through me' as Liz's pregnancy manifesto is absurdly grandiose. The callback to 'Rufus T. Barleysheath is kicking' shows the joke hasn't been abandoned. Strong sequence.

jokes.text: I know you're not pregnant. Why don't you just admit it? / She's grabbing oil. Owen... Run!
jokes.setup: Carmen has finally confronted Liz/Avery at the photo shoot.
jokes.punchline: Avery's warning 'She's grabbing oil. Owen... Run!' — 'Owen' presumably being a photographer — implies Liz is now threatening people with pregnancy oil in a deranged physical confrontation.
jokes.explanation: The image of Liz weaponizing pregnancy oil is funny and escalates the photo shoot absurdity appropriately. 'Owen... Run!' is a good specific detail — we've never heard of Owen, but someone cares about him.

jokes.text: I don't fly, but I got my own bus with a pool table in it. We'll drive to Branson together sometime, take in a Yakov Smirnoff show. Doesn't Russia sound like a crazy place?
jokes.setup: Hank is saying goodbye to Jack and making friendly small talk.
jokes.punchline: Hank's folksy travel plan — not flying, private bus with pool table, Branson, Yakov Smirnoff — is a perfect portrait of a certain kind of wealthy man's anti-cosmopolitan taste. 'Doesn't Russia sound like a crazy place?' is the cherry.
jokes.explanation: The Yakov Smirnoff reference as a destination activity — combined with 'Doesn't Russia sound like a crazy place?' as a genuine question — is excellent character comedy for Hank. He knows Yakov Smirnoff but relates to Russia only as an abstraction.

jokes.text: You do not have a lot of charisma.
jokes.setup: Hank meets Kenneth for the first time.
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate, gentle observation — 'You do not have a lot of charisma' — delivered as an honest assessment rather than an insult, is a perfect Hank line.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Kenneth is actually quite charismatic in his own way, making Hank's assessment wrong as well as blunt. The honest gentleness of the delivery — not mean, just observational — is very Hank.

jokes.text: Here is my letter of resignation. It's probably for the best since this is obviously not a good fit. If you call security to escort me out, you should know I have several pistols hidden on me.
jokes.setup: Jack, shamed by confessing the stolen idea, submits his resignation.
jokes.punchline: The resignation letter is accompanied by a casual warning that Jack is armed — 'I have several pistols hidden on me' — delivered as a simple logistical note for security planning purposes.
jokes.explanation: The casual pistol disclosure as a resignation etiquette note is wonderful Jack Donaghy. 'Several pistols' — the plural — is important. He's not threatening anyone; he's being helpful to security. Highly quotable and excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Kabletown, we're not sharks. We're more like... whatever the friendliest fish is. I'm not a science guy.
jokes.setup: Hank is reassuring Jack that Kabletown operates differently from corporate sharks.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know the name of the friendliest fish — and rather than fake it, he simply says 'I'm not a science guy,' which is both self-deprecating and charming.
jokes.explanation: Hank's admission of ignorance about fish taxonomy, delivered without embarrassment, is consistent with his anti-pretension character. 'I'm not a science guy' as a closer is the right button.

jokes.text: No? How about a hug? / You've gotta be kidding me.
jokes.setup: Kenneth says he doesn't want anything as a reward; Hank offers a hug.
jokes.punchline: Jack's defeated 'You've gotta be kidding me' — watching a hug be offered and accepted as a legitimate business reward — is the perfect reaction to this entire subplot's resolution.
jokes.explanation: Jack's existential defeat at watching a hug constitute a business transaction is a good button on the subplot. His worldview has been completely defeated by genuine kindness.

jokes.text: I can get you into a restaurant where you watch a child play with a bunny, then you eat the bunny.
jokes.setup: Jack is making a final attempt to give Kenneth something valuable in exchange for the idea.
jokes.punchline: The most extravagant reward Jack can think of is a restaurant where the emotional trauma of watching a child bond with a rabbit is followed by eating that same rabbit.
jokes.explanation: One of 30 Rock's all-time great Jack Donaghy absurdisms. The restaurant is described with complete seriousness — Jack presents it as an exclusive privilege rather than a horror. The sequential emotional arc (child plays with bunny → you eat bunny) is dark in a specific, crafted way. The implication that this is a real restaurant that Jack has connections to is the final touch. High quotability and originality. Justifies 9+ scores.

jokes.text: It doesn't count as a hug unless it goes on for ten seconds. / One... Mississippi...
jokes.setup: Hank offers Kenneth a hug.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth insists on a full ten-second hug — echoing Hank's own rule from the episode's opening — and Hank complies, counting aloud.
jokes.explanation: A very satisfying structural callback — Hank introduced the ten-second hug rule at the start of the episode, and now Kenneth deploys it back at Hank. The circle is complete. Good structural writing, and the image of Hank and Kenneth counting together while Jack watches is strong.

jokes.text: Thank you, Lemon. I owe you. If you want to make it up to me, I have my eye on a toilet pillow from a certain medical supply store.
jokes.setup: Avery thanks Liz for covering for her. Liz deflects with her actual reward request.
jokes.punchline: Liz's idea of a thank-you gift is 'a toilet pillow from a certain medical supply store' — an extremely unglamorous and specific desire that Liz has clearly been thinking about for some time.
jokes.explanation: A very Liz Lemon reward request. 'A toilet pillow' is both a real product and an absurd luxury — the kind of unglamorous comfort item that captures Liz perfectly. 'From a certain medical supply store' implies she's already researched it.

jokes.text: Avery and I want the baby's middle name to be Elizabeth, after you. Oh, Jack, that's so gayballs.
jokes.setup: Jack reveals the baby will have Elizabeth as a middle name in honor of Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response to this touching gesture — 'Oh, Jack, that's so gayballs' — is both dismissive and genuinely affectionate, delivered in Liz's particular anti-sentimental register.
jokes.explanation: 'Gayballs' as Liz's term for something touching and sentimental is excellent character comedy — it's her way of accepting sentiment while keeping her guard up. The juxtaposition of the touching gesture and the crude term is the core joke.

jokes.text: Do you need some liniment rubbed on your perineum?
jokes.setup: The staff, still thinking Liz is pregnant, is being solicitous.
jokes.punchline: The offer to rub liniment on Liz's perineum is both medically inappropriate and deeply invasive — delivered with genuine helpfulness.
jokes.explanation: A good cringe joke — the specific anatomical region ('perineum') delivered with sincere helpfulness is where the comedy lives. The earnestness of the offer is the key ingredient.

jokes.text: Why would you pretend to help Jack? Help him for real. It takes the same amount of time.
jokes.setup: Liz has revealed she was only pretending to be pregnant to help Jack.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's logic — 'Why pretend to help? Help for real. It takes the same amount of time' — is both completely correct and reveals that Tracy views helping as a logistical rather than emotional question.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's accidentally profound observation — 'it takes the same amount of time' — is delivered as pure pragmatism but is actually philosophically sound. The humor comes from Tracy being right for completely wrong reasons. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: No, Tracy, she lied to us. And she ordered us around like we were a couple of normals.
jokes.setup: Tracy suggests they let Liz off the hook.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's grievance is being treated 'like normals' — an insult she finds more offensive than the deception itself.
jokes.explanation: 'A couple of normals' as an insult is excellent character work — Jenna and Tracy see being treated like ordinary people as a profound indignity. The word 'normals' (plural noun) is specific and feels right for how they conceive of the distinction between themselves and regular humans.

jokes.text: No, Tracy, she lied to us. And she ordered us around like we were a couple of normals. You will be punished. Can I have my nunchucks back?
jokes.setup: The cast learns Liz was faking pregnancy.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's punishment threat — 'You will be punished' — immediately pivots to the practical matter of recovering her nunchucks, implying punishment by nunchucks and that Liz has them confiscated.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from dramatic proclamation to practical nunchuck recovery is a good structural joke. 'A couple of normals' is also a funny phrase from Jenna. The implication that Liz routinely confiscates Jenna's nunchucks is great background character comedy.

jokes.text: Good God! I have been punished. These are yours to keep.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks for her nunchucks back as punishment for Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately receives the punishment (presumably struck by nunchucks) and immediately surrenders them — 'These are yours to keep' — without even processing what happened.
jokes.explanation: The instant capitulation after a single nunchuck strike is a good physical comedy button. 'These are yours to keep' said in shock is a funny line.

jokes.text: What? Who's the black guy? A bicycle messenger. You took your pants off.
jokes.setup: The scene has apparently descended into chaos off-screen.
jokes.punchline: Liz's rapid-fire questions and observations — a mystery black man, a bicycle messenger, someone removing pants — imply a scene of total chaos she's processing in real time.
jokes.explanation: An absurdist chaos gag — the implied off-screen mayhem is funnier for being unexplained. The three-beat structure (black guy, bicycle messenger, pants) escalates well even though none of it is explained.

jokes.text: What if there was a channel that's just the sound of people having a party so you put it on when you call your parents? / You know what my TV is? A sunset.
jokes.setup: More employee pitch ideas are being presented.
jokes.punchline: First pitch: a fake party soundtrack channel for people ashamed of their quiet lives. Second pitch: 'My TV is a sunset' — a non-pitch that is either profound or meaningless.
jokes.explanation: The 'party sound channel' is a genuinely insightful and funny concept — it addresses a specific social shame with an absurd solution. 'My TV is a sunset' is deliberately meaningless in a way that's funny. Good pitch montage material.

jokes.text: How about a button you push on your remote and you can buy anything you see on TV? Like if you're watching Sex and the City and you just have to have Mr. Big's spaghetti?
jokes.setup: Employee pitch montage continues.
jokes.punchline: The buy-it-now TV remote is a real concept (QVC, interactive TV) — but the specific example chosen is 'Mr. Big's spaghetti' from Sex and the City, a made-up product from a non-product show.
jokes.explanation: The 'Mr. Big's spaghetti' detail is inspired — it's a real show reference but applied to a completely made-up and unglamorous product. The specificity elevates this above the average pitch joke.

jokes.text: What if we executed someone live on TV?
jokes.setup: The pitch montage continues with increasingly unhinged ideas.
jokes.punchline: The cleanest and darkest possible TV pitch: live execution. Delivered with presumably the same earnestness as the others.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — nine words, maximum darkness. The pitch is both absurd and, in the context of reality TV escalation, almost plausible. The structure of the pitch montage means it lands as a pure punchline with no wasted words.

jokes.text: And then I pull off my mask and I'm a lizard person too. Blackout. End of episode.
jokes.setup: The final employee pitch is being given.
jokes.punchline: The pitch ends with 'and then I pull off my mask and I'm a lizard person too' — a conspiracy-theory reveal — followed by the employee narrating 'Blackout. End of episode.' as if describing a screenplay.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly meta ending. 'Blackout. End of episode.' narrated by a character IS the blackout and end of the episode — a perfect meta-referential joke that also works as a conspiracy absurdist pitch. 'I'm a lizard person too' implies the pitch has a prior lizard person reveal we missed. The episode ends on this, which is a bold structural choice that works.

tmdb_overview: As Jack tries to cozy up to the owner of Kabletown, Liz fakes being pregnant to help Avery gain advantage over a competitive colleague. Elsewhere, Tracy and Jenna clash when trying to share a gift from their new bosses.
insight: 88 jokes in 25 minutes hits 30 Rock's absurdist peak at 3.51 per minute.
